Question: How does Himalayan pink salt differ from regular table salt?
Answer: Salt, “sodium chloride,” is naturally snow white. So if the salt is pure, it is white. Himalayan pink salt is pink because it contains pink dirt. Most of the dirt, by analysis, is rust. Fact. “But it’s loaded with valuable minerals” Horse crap. Analysis shows that there isn’t enough of any mineral to be of health significance to a human. You’d have to consume a fatal dose of this dirty salt to get any benefits from it. “But since the crystals are larger, less salt fits in a teaspoon, so you’re eating less sodium.” <slaps forehead> Correct, genius, if less salt fits in your teaspoon because the rest of the space is air, you’re consuming less salt/sodium. Buy your table salt with a coarser grind. No dirt. “But I like the flavor difference.” Most of us grow out of eating dirt, boogers, and library paste. Whatever makes your boat float, I guess. “I like it because it’s less processed.” Processed is a dirty word, literally. The processing of salt is for one purpose — getting rid of the dirt. Nothing is added. Nothing but dirt is taken away. “It’s better because it doesn’t have any additives.” Wait. Wut? What about all of that added dirt? It’s true that no modern company added the dirt but it’s still something foreign added to the sodium chloride. The only additives in plain pure table salt are a safe agent to keep the naturally hygroscopic sodium chloride from turning itself into a solid lump inside your salt shaker, or, in some countries, an iodine compound is added to keep you from developing a nasty ugly affliction called “goiter.” In a few countries, they’ve started to add a fluoride compound to keep the teeth from falling out of your crotch fruit or end up with a mouth full of cavities like you or your parents had. Finally, in most countries, the Himalayan stuff is grotesquely more expensive. That’s a difference. If you’re in one of the rare locations where the pink stuff is the same price as the pure stuff, I’d seriously look at the price of the pure stuff. Somebody is ripping you off.

Question: What’s the most impressive DIY project you’ve completed?
Answer: I bought a 3-level townhouse in the early 1970s in the ‘burbs of Chicago, Illinois, USA. Central heating but no A/C. As many people who know Chicago will tell you, it can get HOT in the summer, with bouts of high humidity adding to the joy. With 2 little ones and a stay-at-home mom, fans just weren’t going to cut it. I got a couple of prices from A/C contractors and choked. No way we could come up with that kind of money. Working for a big construction conglomerate, I knew the company could buy anything under the sun at wholesale. That’s what I did — used the company’s purchasing power to buy all of the components to install central air in my townhouse. Now what? DIY. Gawd what a project. Had to form and pour a concrete pad outside for the main compressor unit. Cutting holes in the furnace plenum duct and riveting in mounting rails for the heat exchanger. Mounting, hosing, and wiring that heavy exchanger. Patching and sealing the plenum. Running the coolant lines from the basement to the outdoor unit. Running wiring for the 240v system, including disconnect and breakers. My Dad and I did it all over a LONG weekend. (Actually, 2 weeks because the poured concrete had to set up for the outside pad.) It almost worked. You see, Dad was old school. Harder, stronger, tighter was always better. Pipe joints had to be twisted until his muscles quivered. So at the electrical junction boxes, the little fittings that thread into the boxes to accept the BX wiring armor had little set screws to lock down on the armor to avoid future pull-outs. I’m watching Dad tighten screws and he’s “gettin’ on ‘em”. “Dang, Dad, do they have to be that tight?” (I was 25 then so I could cuss around Dad without a swat up side my head.) “Oh, yeah, you don’t want that metal slipping apart.” So we wrapped up the job and it was time for the electrical “smoke test” where you throw the connection live for the first time. BIZZZZZZCHT!!! Sparks and smoke were flying all over the basement. After a quick disconnecting, it was found that “Strongman” had tightened one retainer screw so far and hard that it had squashed the BX armoring down into the wiring insulation, leading to a dead short to the electrical box. Geez. Dad was sheepish. Not a terribly hard fix and we had cold air that night. The next week I went around loosening electric box BX screws just a bit and checking with a flashlight to look for any other crushed joints. None. It worked fine for a couple of years that we lived there. Then we moved on.

Question: What is the best method for sealing leaks in stainless steel pipes?

Question: What preventive measures should be taken to avoid mosquito bites?
Answer: I worked in mosquito hell for many years. In all that time I very rarely got any bites and only got one serious mosquito-borne illness, late in life after getting a bit careless. Do this … Avoid going outdoors at dawn or dusk when they’re most aggressively feeding (biting). Keep your indoor area well-screened. Wear light-colored clothing, covering as much of your body as tolerable. Do NOT go out wearing perfumes or odiferous aftershaves, body creams, etc. Apply DEET-containing repellent with a concentration of 20% or higher (in the jungle, we always used 100% DEET). Go for the modern time-release formulations, if you can find them. If you are sensitive to DEET, or it is damaging your clothing (plastics) then use Picaridin repellents but you’ll have to reapply them as often as every 4 hours. The application should be all over your skin and clothing. Several of the most dangerous types of mosquito can bite right through a surprising thickness of modern clothing. Don’t believe most of the labels that say “12-hour protection”. That is bull pucky. DEET is generally good for 8 hours unless you’re pouring sweat. Picaridin is only “excellent” for about 4 hours — then performance starts to plummet. All of the others start allowing bites in from 1 to 4 hours. Many of the voodoo “natural” crap products only work for a tiny window of time, if they do anything at all. Finally, police your property. Find and eliminate any standing water. Old tires and pet watering sites are typical and terrible mosquito breeders.

Question: How do you remove glue gun glue from various surfaces?

Massive areas are made more prone to “failure of the bond” and therefore greater ease of removal by taking advantage of any difference in the coefficient of expansion between the adhesive and the spill surface. For example, deep-chilling a steel object with hot melt on it may make the spill just fall off. We’ve used liquid nitrogen quite successfully to do this. Generally, porous surfaces and fabrics will require heat, the correct solvent, and a powerful vacuum. Don’t expect great results. This is where you need to know what type of hot melt you have and probably need the manufacturer’s tech support people to help you.

We would see this in misdesigned subsea equipment where a large stainless object would have one carbon steel bolt or pipe fitting on it. The carbon steel would “go away” astoundingly quickly in the salt water while the stainless remained undamaged. (The same principle is used to protect carbon steel machines and ships’ hulls in saltwater. The steel is “dotted” here and there with the far less noble blocks of zinc. The corrosive action eats the zinc and leaves the steel.) Sadly, we’re getting quite a few stainless steel parts from other countries that is not homogenous and there are isolated islets of iron that were either rolled into the stainless on dirty rollers or formed during the hot phases due to poor mill practices or cheating on the chromium percentages.

Question: How are metal shims made?
Answer: I’m not sure how they’re commercially manufactured but on an artisan level, they’re made using a rolling mill where a bar of metal is run between two powerful rollers that squeeze the metal thinner. Once thinned a bit the rollers are forced slightly closer together and the thinned bar is run through the rollers again, squeezing it to thinner still. This is repeated until the desired shim thickness is achieved. This is a small shop’s soft metal “roll”. (The lower set of rolls is for rolling shapes to create wires and small rods.) Hard metal shims like steel require even more massive rolls and motor power.

In really horrible areas you may even want a hat with a head net but I always just got away with a few drops of DEET rubbed between my palms and then spread across my neck, forehead, and ears. Question: My silver half dollars smell of mold from being in a moldy safe They are not a collectors item just for investment purposes. Can I get the smell out? What containers should I use use for storage in a safe?

It grows readily on dirt and the oils from your hands from handling the coins. This means that the coins need to be surface cleaned with a solution of DAWN detergent mixed in water, then rinsed in running water, then air dried in a 100C (212F) oven. From now on never touch your coins with your bare hands. Clean (fresh) surgical gloves or cotton gloves that are fresh and probably free of mold spores. All paper items will have to be decontaminated. All other items from the safe must also be thoroughly dowsed with mold-killing spray or treated in the 1-hour oven, thereafter handled with gloves. Place a suitable desiccant pack inside the safe just before returning the coins and other items. Calculate the size of the pack based on its stated protection volume and the calculated internal volume of the safe.
